title: The Karaites today
hookLine: a small community still keeps the written Torah without the rabbinic tradition

cards: Late winter, a field of young barley. A few people walk the rows, stopping to bend down and rub the heads of grain between their fingers. Are they ripe enough?

It matters, because for this community the answer helps decide when the new year of months begins, and so when Passover falls. The Torah calls that season Abib, and they go out to look for it in the field itself.
These are Karaite Jews, a small community that has kept its own path for a very long time.

teach.b: The Karaites today. The principle is simple.

Karaites read the written Torah and the rest of the Hebrew Bible as the authority, without the Oral Torah that rabbinic Judaism holds alongside it, the tradition gathered in the Mishnah and the Talmud.
They point to a verse in Deuteronomy: "Ye shall not add unto the word which I command you, neither shall ye diminish ought from it."

Karaite tradition credits an early teacher with a line often paraphrased as: search the scripture well, and do not lean on my opinion. Each reader is responsible for reading. Here is what that looks like.
The Torah says, "This day came ye out in the month Abib," so Karaites look to the ripening barley and the new moon for their calendar.
And you met this verse with the Law Committee: "Ye shall kindle no fire throughout your habitations upon the sabbath day."

Karaites have traditionally read it to mean no fire left burning on Shabbat, while rabbinic Jews read the same verse, with the Oral Torah, as allowing a light lit before Shabbat begins. Same verse, two readings.
Karaite prayer also includes bowing down fully, the whole body to the ground.

And the last word of today's title: today. Karaites are not a chapter in a history book. There are Karaite synagogues and families now, in Israel and elsewhere, keeping their festivals by the field and the moon.
Rabbinic Jews and Karaites have argued long and hard, and this lesson need not settle it.
It only needs to say the plain thing: a community that reads the Torah its own way is still here.

how: Karaite Jews keep the commandments of the Hebrew Bible as they read them directly, set their calendar by the new moon and the ripening barley, and pray in their own synagogues, including full prostration.

practice: Choose one picture from today: the barley rubbed between fingers, the Shabbat with no flame burning, or the whole body bowed to the ground in prayer.
Hold it, and notice what it would be like to keep it, week after week, faithfully, as a small community while the neighbors around you do something else.
